190.title: Thou hast searched me (Psalm 138 [139])
190.hook: you knit me in my mother's womb, and there's nowhere God is not
190.tomorrow: let every spirit praise the Lord
190.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 138 [139] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and a verse of it forms the traditional entrance chant of Easter Sunday; many pray its closing lines before an examination of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the rivers of Babylon: exiles weeping, and rage handed to God. Your line was even anger can be prayed. Did you try it? Today, a psalm about being seen all the way through. Day one hundred ninety.

There's a particular kind of fear in being fully known. Most of us keep a few rooms locked. The thing we did at nineteen. The thought we'd never say out loud. The version of us that shows up at two in the morning. We let people see the front hallway and keep the rest shut. And there's a particular kind of loneliness in never being known at all. Today's psalm lives right between those two feelings. It says: you have been seen in every room, and you have not been walked out on. Today: thou hast searched me.
screen: `A FEW LOCKED ROOMS.` → `AFRAID OF BEING KNOWN.` → `LONELY IF WE'RE NOT.`

segments.voice: The title comes from the King James: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me." The Douay-Rheims says proved me, tested like metal. The Hebrew is chakar, to search out, to dig to the bottom. First, known. The psalmist says God knows when he sits down and gets up, knows his thoughts from far off, knows the word on his tongue before he says it. That could sound like surveillance. It doesn't read like that. It reads like wonder. Second, nowhere God is not. "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there." Up, down, the far side of the sea, the dark itself: the psalmist tries every exit and finds God already there, not to trap him, but to hold him. Even the darkness, he says, isn't dark to you. Third, made. "Thou hast covered me in my mother's womb. I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Before anyone else knew you existed, the psalm says, you were known. Catholics hear this psalm on Easter morning: the old entrance chant of Easter Sunday, Resurrexi, comes from a verse of it, I arose, and am still with thee. And the psalm ends where it started, but now as a request: search me, O God, and know my heart. The same knowing that could have been frightening becomes something he asks for.
screen: `CHAKAR: DUG TO THE BOTTOM.` · `NOWHERE GOD IS NOT.` · `KNOWN BEFORE YOU WERE BORN.` · `FROM FEAR TO SEARCH ME.` · then, large: `I AM FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in being fully known. Settle, and breathe. Think of one of your locked rooms. You don't have to open it or name it out loud. Just let yourself know it's there. Then, if you pray, rest in the psalm's claim that God has already seen that room and hasn't left. You can say its last words: search me, O God, and know my heart. If you don't pray, simply breathe, and let yourself be all of who you are for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Thou hast searched me. The first words of the psalm about being known completely, everywhere, from before birth, and still held. Today's word.
Your line: known, and not left. Today, let one person see a little more of you than usual, or be someone who stays when you see more of them. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Let every spirit praise the Lord (Psalm 150)
191.hook: trumpets, harp, timbrel, cymbals, and everything that breathes
191.howItsDone: Catholics sing the Alleluia before the Gospel at Mass, omit it through Lent, and bring it back at the Easter Vigil; Psalm 150 is prayed at Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thou hast searched me: seen in every room, and still held. Your line was known, and not left. Who stayed? Today, the last psalm of all. Day one hundred ninety-one.

Think of the end of a great concert. The last song. Everyone on stage plays at once: drums, horns, strings, the whole choir, and the crowd is on its feet, singing along. Nobody's holding back anything for later, because there is no later. That's how the book of Psalms ends. A hundred fifty psalms of joy and grief, anger and trust, and the very last one is a finale where every instrument comes in, and then the music hands itself to anyone with breath in their lungs. Today's word is the one it's built on: Alleluia.
screen: `THE LAST SONG OF THE NIGHT.` → `EVERY INSTRUMENT AT ONCE.` → `THEN, EVERYONE WHO BREATHES.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Alleluia is Hebrew, hallelu-Yah: hallelu, all of you, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name. So it isn't a feeling, it's an invitation: everybody, praise God. It came into Greek and Latin untranslated, and Catholics still sing it that way today. Second, the orchestra. Psalm 150 is six verses and almost every line is a call to praise. It moves out from the sanctuary to the sky, then through the band. In the Douay-Rheims: "Praise him with sound of trumpet: praise him with psaltery and harp." Then timbrel and dancing, strings and pipes, cymbals, loud cymbals. It's the most joyful noise in the Bible. Third, the last line. After all the instruments, it lands on the one instrument everybody has. "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." The Hebrew says everything that has breath. The Latin and the Douay say spirit, and it's the same idea: breath and spirit are linked words in both languages. You don't need a trumpet. You need lungs. Fourth, how Catholics keep this word. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel at Mass. But through the whole of Lent, the Church goes without it. On Easter night, at the Vigil, it comes back, sung three times, rising each time. So this is the end of our Psalms. Over thirty-five days we walked from the two ways of Psalm one, through the shepherd, the Miserere, the pilgrims' road, the depths and the rivers of exile, to a finale where everything that breathes is invited to join.
screen: `HALLELU-YAH: EVERYBODY, PRAISE GOD.` · `TRUMPET, HARP, TIMBREL, CYMBALS.` · `THE LAST INSTRUMENT: BREATH.` · `SILENT IN LENT, BACK AT EASTER.` · then, large: `LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow alleluia. Settle, and breathe. Notice your breath going in and out on its own, without you asking. Now, on one long out-breath, let the word ride out quietly: al-le-lu-ia. Then just breathe for a while, and do it again when you're ready. If you pray, it's praise. If you don't, it's simply a long, slow breath out, noticing that you're alive. The bell holds the time.
Alleluia. From the Hebrew hallelu-Yah: all of you, praise God. The word the Psalms end on. Today's word.

Your line: everything that breathes. Today, notice one living thing breathing, a dog asleep, a baby, a bird, the person next to you, and count it in the choir. Tomorrow we open a gospel and read it straight through. Day one hundred ninety-one.

192.title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
192.hook: no birth story, just the beginning of the good news and a voice in the desert
192.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics stand for the Gospel, trace a small cross on forehead, lips and heart as it is announced, and hear it read by a deacon or priest; the Gospel of Mark is read on most Sundays in Year B of the lectionary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alleluia, and the Psalms ended with everything that breathes. That was your line. Did you count someone into the choir? Today we open a new book, and read it straight through. Day one hundred ninety-two.

Most stories about a famous person start with a birth. A baby, a family, a hometown, a childhood. Matthew and Luke do that: angels, shepherds, wise men, a stable. Mark doesn't. No manger. No star. No Mary and Joseph on the road. Mark opens with one line, like a title card at the start of a film, and then drops you straight into the desert, where a wild man in camel's hair is shouting at crowds. For the next forty days we'll read Mark from start to finish, a few verses at a time. Today's word is the one in his first sentence: gospel.
screen: `NO MANGER. NO STAR.` → `ONE LINE, LIKE A TITLE CARD.` → `FORTY DAYS OF MARK.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole first verse. Mark tells you what he's writing and who it's about, and doesn't waste a word. Second, the word. Gospel comes from old English, god-spel, good story, good news. Mark wrote in Greek, and his word is euangelion. In his world it was the word for big public news: a victory announced, a new emperor, a royal birth, sent out by messengers to every town. Greek Isaiah used the same root for heralds running ahead of God, and Paul was already using the word for the message about Jesus. Mark sets it over the whole story. This, he says, is the real headline. Third, the voice. Mark quotes the prophets: "A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." And there's John the Baptist, living rough, dressed in camel's hair with a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, calling people to be baptized in the Jordan and to turn their lives around. Crowds come out from the whole countryside and from Jerusalem. And then John points away from himself. Someone mightier is coming after me, he says; I'm not worthy to stoop down and untie his sandals. Fourth, the book. Mark is the shortest of the four gospels. Many scholars think it was the first written, and an early tradition says Mark set down what he'd heard Peter preach. You can read it aloud in about two hours. It moves fast. We'll feel that tomorrow.
screen: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.` · `EUANGELION: PUBLIC GOOD NEWS.` · `A VOICE CRYING IN THE DESERT.` · `THE SHORTEST GOSPEL, AND FAST.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first line aloud. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible or your phone nearby, find Mark chapter one, verse one. If not, use the words you heard: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Say it out loud, slowly, the way a herald would announce news in a town square. Then sit with it. What would good news sound like, for you, today? If you pray, you can offer that. The bell holds the time.
Gospel. Old English for good news, from the Greek euangelion, the word for news big enough to send heralds. Today's word.
Your line: gospel means good news. Today, be the one who carries good news to someone: a thank-you, a well done, a thing that went right. Day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: Straight into the desert (Mark 1:9–13)
193.hook: baptism, the voice, then the Spirit drives him out among the wild beasts
193.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that closes the Christmas season, and hear Mark's short account of the forty days in the desert on the First Sunday of Lent in Year B.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beginning of Mark, and the word gospel. Your line was gospel means good news. Whose good news did you carry? Today, Jesus walks into the story. Day one hundred ninety-three.

Some storytellers linger. They give you the weather, the smell of the kitchen, what everyone was wearing. Mark is not one of them. Mark is the friend who tells a story so fast you have to say, wait, back up. In five verses today, Jesus arrives from a small village, is baptized in a river, sees the sky rip open, hears a voice, and is driven out into the wilderness for forty days. Five verses. Mark has a favorite word for this speed, and you're going to start hearing it everywhere. Today: straight into the desert.
screen: `SOME STORYTELLERS LINGER.` → `MARK DOES NOT.` → `FIVE VERSES, FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the river. Jesus comes from Nazareth in Galilee, a village nobody would have expected, and John baptizes him in the Jordan. Mark doesn't stop to explain why. He just moves. Second, the word. The King James puts it like this: "And straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him." Straightway. In Greek it's euthys, immediately, right then. Mark uses it over and over, around forty times in sixteen chapters. Watch for it. It gives his whole gospel the feeling of running. Third, the sky. Where the English says opened, Mark's Greek actually says the heavens were torn, ripped like cloth. And a voice from heaven says: you are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased. Catholics see the whole Trinity in this moment: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. Fourth, the desert. And then, immediately again. In the Douay-Rheims: "And immediately the Spirit drove him out into the desert." Drove is a strong word, the same word Mark later uses for driving out demons. Jesus is there forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serve him. That's it. Mark gives one sentence. He doesn't tell us what the temptations were; Matthew and Luke do that. Mark is silent, and only Mark mentions the wild beasts. Beloved, and straight into the wilderness: in Mark, being loved by God doesn't mean an easy road. It means the road starts right away.
screen: `A VILLAGE NOBODY EXPECTED.` · `EUTHYS: STRAIGHTWAY.` · `THE HEAVENS TORN OPEN.` · `DRIVEN INTO THE WILDERNESS.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT DROVE HIM OUT INTO THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how fast Mark moves, and how fast you do. Settle, and breathe. Replay your morning in your head, quickly: woke up, and straightway, phone. And straightway, coffee. And straightway, the next thing. Notice how few pauses there were. Now, for these two minutes, don't go straightway anywhere. Stay put. If you pray, you can rest in the words spoken over Jesus at the river: beloved. If you don't, just rest. The bell holds the time.
Straight into the desert. From the river to the wilderness in a single breath: Jesus's baptism and his forty days, told Mark's way. Today's word.
Your line: straightway. Today, every time you hear yourself rushing, say the word in your head, and see if one thing can wait a breath. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Fishers of men (Mark 1:14–20)
194.hook: the kingdom is at hand, and fishermen leave their nets
194.howItsDone: Catholics hear the call of the first disciples at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the pope wears the Ring of the Fisherman as a sign of succession to Saint Peter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, straight into the desert: the river, the torn sky, the forty days. Your line was straightway. Did anything wait a breath? Today, the first followers. Day one hundred ninety-four.

Early morning on a lake in Galilee. Two brothers are standing in the shallows, throwing a round net out over the water, pulling it back, throwing it again. It's what their father did. It's what they'll do tomorrow. Down the shore, two more brothers are sitting in their father's boat, mending torn nets, the most ordinary job there is. Nobody's praying. Nobody's looking for a change. And a man walks along the beach, stops, and says two words that will take all four of them away from that shore for the rest of their lives. Today: fishers of men.
screen: `A LAKE AT DAWN.` → `CASTING NETS, MENDING NETS.` → `A MAN WALKS ALONG THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: First, the announcement. John the Baptist has been arrested, and Jesus comes into Galilee with a message you can say in one breath. In the Douay-Rheims: "The time is accomplished, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel." At hand means close enough to touch. Repent, in Greek metanoia, means more than feeling sorry. It means turning your mind around, facing a new way. Second, the call. Jesus sees Simon and his brother Andrew casting their nets into the sea, and says: "Come after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men." He uses their own work. You catch fish; now you'll gather people. Third, the leaving. And, Mark's favorite word again: "And immediately leaving their nets, they followed him." A little further on he calls James and John, the sons of Zebedee, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men and go. Notice what Mark doesn't say. He doesn't say whether they'd heard Jesus preach before. He doesn't say what they felt, or what their father said. John's gospel suggests some of them had met Jesus earlier; Mark just shows the leaving. Fourth, why Catholics care. Simon is the one Jesus will call Peter, and Catholics see in him the first of the popes. To this day, every pope wears a ring called the Ring of the Fisherman, a reminder that the Church began on a beach with men who dropped their nets.
screen: `THE KINGDOM IS AT HAND.` · `COME AFTER ME.` · `THEY LEFT THEIR NETS AND FATHER.` · `THE RING OF THE FISHERMAN.` · then, large: `I WILL MAKE YOU TO BECOME FISHERS OF MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one small net. Settle, and breathe. Think about the thing that keeps pulling your hands and eyes all day: the phone, the news, a game, a feed. Picture it as a net you keep casting. Now put it down, physically if you can, face down, out of reach, for these two minutes. If you pray, you can listen for what might be calling you instead. If you don't, just notice how your hands feel empty, and let them rest. The bell holds the time.
Fishers of men. Jesus's call to Simon and Andrew: leave catching fish, and gather people instead. Today's word.
Your line: they left their nets. Today, leave one small distraction behind for an hour and see who or what you notice instead. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: A day in Capernaum (Mark 1:21–39)
195.hook: teaching, healing late into the night, and before dawn he goes out alone to pray
195.howItsDone: Many Catholics keep a morning prayer before the day begins, such as Morning Prayer from the Liturgy of the Hours or a morning offering; monks and nuns rise before dawn for the early Office.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fishers of men: four fishermen on a beach, and a call. Your line was they left their nets. What did you put down? Today, their first day together. Day one hundred ninety-five.

You know those days that never stop. Out the door early, one thing after another, people needing you, the phone going, and by the time you sit down it's dark and you can't remember lunch. Mark gives us one of those days in the life of Jesus, almost hour by hour, in a small fishing town on the lake called Capernaum. Morning in the synagogue. Afternoon at Simon's house. Evening, the whole town at the door. And then, the next morning, something that tells you how he got through it. Today: a day in Capernaum.
screen: `A DAY THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `CAPERNAUM, HOUR BY HOUR.` → `AND THE NEXT MORNING.`

segments.voice: First, the morning. It's the sabbath, and Jesus teaches in the synagogue. People are stunned, Mark says, because he teaches with authority, not like the scribes, who quoted other teachers. A man with an unclean spirit cries out, and Jesus silences the spirit and sends it out. Second, the afternoon. They go to the house of Simon and Andrew. Simon's mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. Jesus goes to her, takes her by the hand, and lifts her up, and the fever leaves her. That small detail tells you something else: Peter had a wife. Third, the evening. When the sun sets, the sabbath is over, and people are free to carry the sick. The whole town gathers at the door. Mark says he healed many, late into the night. Fourth, the dawn. Here's the verse. In the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." Before anyone's up, after the biggest day yet, he slips out alone. Mark doesn't tell us what he prayed. He just tells us he went. And they come hunting for him. Simon finds him and says, almost impatiently: "All seek for thee." You'd expect Jesus to go back to the crowd that loves him. He doesn't. He says, let's go on to the next towns, so I can preach there too; that's why I came. Visitors to Capernaum today can see the ruins of an old synagogue, and nearby, under a modern church, the remains of a house Christians have honored since early times as Peter's.
screen: `MORNING: TEACHING WITH AUTHORITY.` · `AFTERNOON: A HAND, AND THE FEVER GOES.` · `EVENING: THE WHOLE TOWN AT THE DOOR.` · `DAWN: ALONE, TO PRAY.` · then, large: `AND RISING VERY EARLY, THERE HE PRAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray early, before anything. If it's morning where you are, good. If not, imagine it's tomorrow, before the alarm, before the phone. Settle, and breathe. Picture a quiet place, like the deserted spot where Jesus went. Nothing to answer yet. Nobody seeking you yet. If you pray, you can simply be with God there, without asking for anything. If you don't, just rest in the quiet before the day's first demand. The bell holds the time.
A day in Capernaum. One full day of Jesus's work in a lake town, from synagogue to sickbed to the crowded door, and then prayer before dawn. Today's word.
Your line: rising very early. Tomorrow morning, before you check anything, give the first few minutes to quiet. Day one hundred ninety-five.

196.title: If thou wilt (Mark 1:40–45)
196.hook: a leper kneels, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches him
196.howItsDone: Catholics hear the healing of the leper at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and many honor saints who served people with leprosy, such as Francis of Assisi and Damien of Molokai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a day in Capernaum, and prayer before dawn. Your line was rising very early. Did you get a few quiet minutes before the day grabbed you? Day one hundred ninety-six.

Think about the last time someone hugged you. Or put a hand on your shoulder. Or just brushed your arm when they laughed. Now imagine years without any of that. Nobody comes near you. When you walk down a road, you're required to call out a warning so people can step away. Your family lives in town and you live outside it. That was life for a man with leprosy in Jesus's day. And in today's story, one of them walks right up to Jesus, kneels in the dirt, and says four words. Today: if thou wilt.
screen: `THE LAST TIME SOMEONE TOUCHED YOU.` → `YEARS WITHOUT IT.` → `A MAN KNEELS IN THE DIRT.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Leprosy in the Bible covered many skin diseases, not only the one we call leprosy today. The law of Moses, in Leviticus, said a person with it had to live outside the camp and cry out unclean. So this man shouldn't be anywhere near Jesus. He comes anyway. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Notice he doesn't doubt Jesus can. He isn't sure Jesus wants to. Plenty of people know that fear. Second, the touch. "And Jesus having compassion on him, stretched forth his hand; and touching him, saith to him: I will. Be thou made clean." He touches him before he heals him. He didn't need to; elsewhere Jesus heals with a word. And under the law, touching a leper made you unclean too. Jesus reaches out anyway. For a man who hadn't been touched in years, the touch may have been the first healing. Third, the word compassion. Mark's Greek is splanchnistheis, moved in the gut, a feeling from deep inside. A few very old manuscripts say something different here: moved with anger. Scholars still argue about which is original. Either way, Jesus is deeply moved. Fourth, the swap. Jesus tells the man to show himself to the priest, as Moses commanded, and to tell no one. The man tells everyone. And now Jesus can't openly enter a town, and stays out in deserted places. The man is back inside; Jesus is outside. Twelve hundred years later, Saint Francis of Assisi wrote that his new life began among lepers, and his early biographers say he kissed one. This week began with the psalm about being known, and ends here: with a hand reaching out to touch.
screen: `OUTSIDE THE CAMP, CRYING UNCLEAN.` · `HE TOUCHES BEFORE HE HEALS.` · `MOVED IN THE GUT.` · `THE MAN IN, JESUS OUT.` · then, large: `I WILL. BE THOU MADE CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a kind touch. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone in your life who doesn't get touched much. An older neighbor who lives alone, a grandparent in a care home, someone who's sick, someone grieving, a kid who's been left out. See their face. If you pray, you can hold them before God, and say the leper's words for them: if thou wilt. If you don't, just decide how you might reach them today: a hand on the arm, a hug, or a visit. The bell holds the time.
If thou wilt. The leper's words to Jesus: sure he could heal, unsure he'd want to. And Jesus answers, I will. Today's word.

Your line: he touched him. This week ran from thou hast searched me and Alleluia into Mark: the gospel, the desert, the nets, Capernaum, and now a touch. Today, reach out kindly to someone who's kept at a distance. Day one hundred ninety-six.
